The comments of the Ministry were received on 19th May 1999. The points raised in thequestionnaire and the comments of the Ministry thereon are as follows: -
Question No.1
The Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act, 1987 provides for compulsory useof Jute materials in packaging of different commodities. It was enacted obviously to protect the dying juteindustry which accounts for subsistence of over 4 million marginal jute farmers and huge work force engaged injute industry and their dependants in the face of challenge from plastic any nylon bag and packaging industry.The vires of the Act were
14
challenged by the plastic and other modern packaging industries and was upheld by the Apex Court. Despite allthis, the very purpose of the
Act is sort to be defeated by way of issue of statutory orders under the act by substantially curtailing the list ofitems which under the Act are to be compulsorily packed in jute. Under S.O. No. 1076 (E) dated 15.12.1998,cement, a major item required to be packed in jute, has been withdrawn from the list and the provision forcompulsory packaging (i) in respect of urea has been reduced by 30% from 50% to 20% and (ii) in respect ofsugar by 20%. There is, thus, a blatant violation of the very spirit of law in issuing the said Statutory order.
What are the comments of the Ministry of Textiles in this behalf?
Reply
The Jute Packaging Materials (Compulsory use in Packing Commodities) Act, 1987 {Section 4 (2)} provides thatthe Standing Advisory Committee shall, after considering the following matters, indicate its recommendations tothe Central Government, namely:
h. the existing level of usage of jute material;
i. the quantity of raw jute, available;
j. the quantity of jute material available;
k. the protection of interests of persons engaged in the jute industry and in the production of raw jute;
l. the need for continued maintenance of jute industry;
m. the quantity of commodities which, in its opinion, is likely to be required for packing in jute material;
n. such other matters as the Standing Advisory Committee may think fit.
The Committee kept in view the above provisions of the Act, and after considering the detailed data provided bythe Jute Commissioner, the conflicting views expressed by concerned Government Departments, user industries,other concerned sectors/bodies, which included various organisations and bodies in the jute sector also, and theState Governments, made certain recommendation to the
15
Government. After considering these recommendations, in detail, in consultation with the concerned Departments,the mater was submitted
to the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs. Based on the decision of CCEA, the Ministry of Textiles notifiedthe Jute Packaging Order of 15.12.1998.

It needs to be further elaborated that the Standing Advisory Committee based its recommendations on thedemand & supply position of jute goods which showed that while the installed capacity of the Industry is 11.00lakh MTs for sacking, the actual production of sacking has been 6.67 lakh MTs and 8.65 lakh MTs in 1996-97 and1997-98 which was barely enough to cover the demand of 6.56 lakh MTs of sacking required for foodgrains, sugarand other export item in 1996-97 and 8.67 lakh MTs in 1997-98 and there was nothing left for the cement industryat all. Similarly the projected figures for 1998-99 and 1999-2000 show that against a projected demand of 8.58lakh of MTs in 1998-99 and 9.56 MTs in 1999-2000 for foodgrains, sugar etc., the production is expected to be ofthe order of 8.50 lakh MTs and 8.75 lakh MTs respectively. Hence in these two years also the jute industry wouldbarely be able to meet the demand of foodgrains and sugar etc. and there will be nothing left for the cementindustry. The commodity wise position is further explained below:-
Cement
The cement industry has been demanding total exemption from the reservation, which provided for 50% ofcement production to be packed in jute packaging. The compliance also in this case has been almost negligible inthe last so many years. They based their demand on certain factors like high seepage in jute bags, health hazardduring packing, jute packaging being costlier than HDPE/PP bags and the fact that sufficient quantity of jutepackaging material was not available for the cement sector. The demand and supply scenario discussed earlieralso indicates the lack of availability for sufficient quantity jute packaging material for cement. Hence it has beendecided to exempt cement from the purview of this reservation order although this

Urea
The fertilizer industry as well as the Department of Fertilizer had wanted urea to be totally exempted from thepurview of this Reservation Order. They argued that the compulsory Packaging of 50% of urea productioninvolves additional outgo of subsidy to the extent of Rs. 100 crores per annum and the consumer prefers HDPEbags instead of Jute bags for urea packaging. It is a fact that on account of jute packaging which is much morecostly than HDPE bags, on the one hand the consumer was burdened with higher price while on the other, to makeurea available at reasonable prices the Government had to provide subsidy of the order of Rs. 100 crores or sounder the administered price mechanism for urea. Hence, in a way a cross subsidization was going on which wasneither in the interest of the consumer nor the Government. Hence it was decided to reduce the percentage ofcompulsory packaging of urea in jute packaging to 20%. Question 1
Whether the order has been laid on the Table of both the Houses of Parliament? If so, the details in this regard?
 
Reply
As per Sub Section 3 of Section 49 of the Tea Act 1953, every rule made under the Act is required to be laid before each House of the Parliament within aperiod of thirty days and accordingly, it is presumed that the Tea (Marketing) Control Order 1984 must have been laid before both the Houses of Parliament.However, in the absence of old records it is not possible to indicate the date on which the Control Order has been laid in the Houses.
Question 2
Tea Act was enacted in the year 1953 whereas the Tea (Marketing) Control Order was issued in the year 1984. How the marketing of tea was controlledduring this long period from 1953 to 1984 and why there has been so much of delay in formulating this Order?
  
28
Reply
Tea Act came into being in the year 1953. Tea was covered by International Tea Agreement during that time. India was a member of the said InternationalAgreement. The said agreement stipulated various terms and conditions to be abided by each of the signatory. The main objective of the said agreement wasto regulate promotion of tea under a quota system to be followed by the tea producing countries. The said agreement ceased to operate in the year 1955 butthe promotion of tea both domestic as well as overseas continued beyond 1955. The domestic promotion of tea in India continued till early half of Sixties.Tea as a beverage within India started picking up steadily. In the year 1978 Government of India felt the necessity of including tea within the ambit ofEssential Commodity under the Essential Commodities Act 1955. The reason for inclusion of tea within the ambit of Essential Commodity Act was aimed atfair and equitable distribution of tea to consumers. Tea continues to be an item under the Essential Commodities Act till today. Tea after 1978 was freelyavailable in the domestic markets but possibility of unfair competition amongst traders in tea was also reported/felt. In order to ensure consumption andexport of tea to overseas markets, a fair and reasonable regulatory mechanism was felt Essential so that the producers gets fair & reasonable price of theirproduct as well as the buyers get a remunerative and competitive price for tea bought by them from the open market. Mandatory Public Action System of tea.Registration of Tea Factories, Licence to Tea Brokers & Tea Auctioneers were brought under a single umbrella and Tea (Marketing) Control Order wasenacted for that purpose. The Tea (Marketing) Control Order 1984 has been successfully in operation till date. The Hon’ble Division Bench of Madras HighCourt has upheld the constitutionality and legality of this Order. Thus this Order with the enabling provisions available under the Tea Act was formulated atthe appropriate time.
